title: From question to answer: what happens inside an AI model

audience.who: Corporate employees in non-technical roles who already use or will soon use AI chat assistants at work
audience.knows: How to type a question into a chat tool and read the reply; little or nothing about how the reply is produced
audience.cares_about: Whether they can trust an answer, why the same question gives different replies, and how to use the tool well

outcome: After watching, the viewer can explain in plain words how an AI assistant builds its reply one predicted piece at a time, and can decide when an answer needs checking because it sounds sure but may be wrong.
through_line: An AI model does not look up an answer; it writes one, a likely next piece at a time, from the words in front of it, so a fluent reply is a prediction, and that is exactly why it can vary and why it can be wrong.

arc_plan.what: A colleague asks an AI assistant the same work question twice and gets two different, equally confident answers; one contains a detail that is not true. Puzzle: what is going on inside?
Follow that one question through the model, step by step, so the viewer sees where the answer really comes from.
Section 1: the question is split into tokens, small pieces of text the model works with as numbers.
Section 2: the model weighs the whole context, deciding which earlier pieces matter most for what comes next.
Section 3: it predicts a likely next token from probabilities, adds it, and repeats until the answer is done; sampling is why replies vary.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: next-token prediction and sampling

arc_plan.what: Section 4: why answers can be wrong: the model produces likely text, not checked truth, so it can give fluent, confident errors, and its knowledge stops at its training data.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: hallucination and training cutoff

arc_plan.what: The viewer judges a short scenario: which of two replies needs verification and why, using the predict-not-look-up idea.
Return to the colleague's two answers, now explained: variation from sampling, the false detail from prediction without checking; what the colleague does next.

must_cover.what: Text is split into tokens (word pieces) that the model represents as numbers
The model uses the context (the question and the conversation so far) and weighs which parts matter for the next token
The answer is generated one token at a time by predicting a probable next token and repeating
Answers vary because the next token is chosen from probabilities, not fixed
Answers can be wrong: fluent, confident text that is not true, because the model predicts likely text rather than checking facts
What the viewer does about it: check important claims, give clear context in the question

must_avoid: Hype or doom about AI; no claims about AI being conscious or understanding like a person
Statistics or model sizes without a source on the knowledge sheet
Vendor or product names presented as endorsement
Technical jargon left unexplained (vectors, transformers named without a plain meaning)
Opening by explaining terms first, or with an agenda; 'in this video we will'
Learning-styles claims and invented attributions to real people
example_posture: One running example the whole lesson follows: a single ordinary work question an office employee would really ask an assistant (a short request about a policy or a summary). Every section shows that same question at its next stage inside the model; no new examples per section.
visual_direction: Make the inside of the model visible as a calm, luminous projected space: the question breaking into pieces, lines of weight connecting the pieces that matter, a short ranked list of candidate next words with their likelihoods, the answer growing word by word. One or two striking moments (the question dissolving into tokens; the same question branching into two different answers), calm uncluttered explanation between them. A person at a desk anchors the start and the end.
voice_note: A capable colleague explaining over coffee: plain, precise, no hype and no condescension. Name each idea only after the viewer has seen it happen.
open_questions: Topic mode with no source document: every build claim must be grounded in the knowledge sheet the fact-finder produces; segments marked from_user rely on the request's topic statement.
Whether to mention retrieval or web search tools that let some assistants look things up; kept out unless the knowledge sheet supports a short caveat.

from_request: notes: plain language, no hype, inside of the model visible and grounded, one or two striking moments
